## Overview

The Serer, also called *Seereer* or *Sereer*, are a West African ethnoreligious group and nation concentrated in Senegal, especially the west-central region from the southern edge of Dakar to the border of The Gambia. They also live in northern Gambia and southern Mauritania. Their traditions trace origins to the Senegal River Valley, at the border of present-day Senegal and Mauritania, followed by migrations southward. The Serer are the third-largest ethnic group in Senegal, making up 16% of its population. Their language belongs to the Senegambian branch of the Niger–Congo family. Serer folk culture includes mixed-farming, distinctive religious symbolism, wrestling, music, oral history, sacred trees, initiation rites and ceremonies connected with the pangool, ancestral spirits and saints.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Sër / serr** — The Serer traditional attire is called *sër* or *serr*, with *pay* given as a Serer proper term. The source says it is normally woven by Serer men and is believed to bring good luck to those who wear it.

### Clothing & dress

The named Serer traditional attire is *sër / serr*, also associated with the Serer proper term *pay*. It is normally woven by Serer men and is believed to bring good luck to its wearer.

Serer religious practice also records forms of bodily and ritual adornment. Serers may wear an item belonging to an ancestor, such as an ancestor’s hair or a treasured belonging, converting it into *juju* worn on the person or visibly around the neck. In Serer society, married women braid their hair in a particular style restricted to married women and treated as a symbol of status.

### Architecture

The sources describe Serer homes as being built according to symbolic principles. In the countryside, a room or hut separate from the main house is built to store excess harvest, including millet, vegetables and other food. People in need know which building to visit and may take what they need without asking permission. The same building structure is said to recur in many traditional Serer homes, although those living in large cosmopolitan cities may not have it.

Serer religious accounts also describe household shrines. In the courtyard of a Serer home, wooden slabs may form a sacred wood representing the centre of divine energies and one of the poles of coronation. Some shrines use raised steles supported by three rods, while others use green trees.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 A *Gamba* is described as a large calabash with a small hollow-out, beaten after the death of an elder as part of funeral regalia. Calabashes also appear in ritual practice, including one containing branches of *Saas* soaked in water, in which Serer men formerly washed their hands after burying the dead.

### Jewelry & body adornment

 They do record ancestral adornment: a person may wear an ancestor’s hair or a treasured belonging as *juju*, either on the body or visibly around the neck. The sources also describe the use of small sticks of *Saas* worn around the waist by young boys and girls to preserve future fertility. At a child’s birth, a *Saas* branch may be placed above the enclosure where the child and mother remain in seclusion for eight days during the *Bat* ceremony.

## Music & performance

Serer music is associated with instruments, vocal traditions and the work of griots. The *sabar* is a drum tradition associated with the Wolof people that the source traces to the Serer Kingdom of Sine before its spread to Saloum and Wolof kingdoms. Its motifs serve different purposes and occasions. Individual motifs represent the history and genealogy of a family and may be used at weddings, naming ceremonies and funerals.

The *Njuup* tradition is identified as a progenitor of Mbalax. The *Tassu* or *Tassou* tradition is identified as a progenitor of rap music and originated among the Serer. It was used when chanting ancient religious verses, with singing interwoven with a *Tassu*. Griots of Senegambia adopted the practice from Serer religious traditions and use it at marriages, naming ceremonies and while praising patrons.

*Lamba* and *sabar* accompany wrestling matches, circumcision dances and royal festivals. The Serer griots preserve oral tradition through songs and music. The *paar no maad*, or chief griot of the king, retained and transmitted royal genealogy and family history, accompanied the king to battle and recounted the glory or bravery of ancestors.

## Dance & theatre

 They do identify circumcision dances and Serer dances as performance contexts. *Lamba* and *sabar* provide musical accompaniment for circumcision dances and royal festivals. Serer wrestling, called *Laamb* or *Njom* in Serer, originated in the Serer Kingdom of Sine and was formerly a preparatory exercise for war among warrior classes.

Wrestling includes several techniques, including *mbapatte*, described as one of the oldest. Children begin with basic techniques before progressing to more advanced forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The *Xooy* or *Xoy* is a special religious event in the Serer calendar. Initiated *Saltigue*, Serer high priests and priestesses, gather before the community to predict the future, including weather, politics and economics. The event brings thousands of people to Holy Sine and usually begins in the first week of June at Fatick. The ceremony may continue for several days, with the *Saltigue* taking centre stage.

The *Raan* festival of Tukar occurs every year on the second Thursday after the appearance of the new moon in April. It takes place in the old village of Tukar, founded by Lamane Jegan Joof. The Lamane prepares offerings of millet, sour milk and sugar, visits the sacred pond and shrine of Saint Luguuñ Joof, and performs offerings of milk, millet, wine and small animals at key shrines, trees and sacred locations.

The annual *A Cuur Ale* ceremony is held in some Serer-Siin villages as a rain ceremony. Representatives of the founding lineage and the village chief pour libations of millet and sugar before the *Saltigues*, who predict future rainfall. The sources also describe the *Daqaar mboob* ceremony, intended to ensure good millet or groundnut production.

Life-cycle practices include the *Bat* ceremony after childbirth, arranged marriages, initiation rites and funerals. During funerals, the *Gamba* is beaten, while a stick of *Saas* may accompany the dead in the tomb. Serer religion observes Monday as a day of rest, while Monday and Thursday are religious days for prayers, offerings and libations to the pangool.

## Foodways

The Serer favourite food is called *chere* or *saay*, described as pounded coos in the Serer language. Serer people control all phases of its production and preparation. It may be eaten with fermented milk or cream and sugar as a breakfast cereal, or prepared as a standard couscous. Other groups may buy it from Serer women market traders or contract them to prepare it for major ceremonial events.

Millet is prominent in Serer foodways and ritual. Offerings at the *Raan* include millet, sour milk and sugar, while the *A Cuur Ale* ceremony uses libations of millet and sugar. The *Daqaar mboob* ceremony is associated with millet or groundnut production. The sources also describe the Serer as farmers, fishers, boat builders and animal keepers, with fishing especially associated with the Serer-Niominka.

Serer homes may contain a separate room or hut for excess harvest, including millet, vegetables and other food, intended for people in need. In some communities, families cook and bring food to the local square so the community can eat together.

## Oral tradition & literature

Serer oral tradition preserves migration narratives, religious teachings, royal genealogies and creation mythology. The creation myth is transmitted through *A nax*, a short narrative or proverbial expression, and *A leep*, a more developed account of the mythical creation word and the creation itself. These sources describe Roog or Koox, the three primordial worlds of water, air and earth, the creation of trees and animals, and the emergence of the first human couple.

The oral tradition includes accounts of Serer resistance to Islamization and stories such as that of the Serer bowman Amar Godomat, who is said to have shot and killed Abu-Bakr Ibn-Umar with an arrow. Griots preserve genealogy and family history through songs and music. The *paar no maad* served as the king’s chief griot and recounted ancestral glory and bravery in battle.

Serer religious chants and poems are part of traditional practice, including verses performed through the *Tassu*.

## Language & religion

Serer belongs to the Senegambian branch of the Niger–Congo family. It includes regional dialects such as Serer-Sine and Serer-Saloum. The source lists Serer Sine, Segum, Fadyut-Palmerin, Dyegueme and Niominka. Serer is primarily written in the Latin alphabet. Historically, an Arabic-based writing system was also used; the *Serer Ajami script* has 29 letters.

Serer religion is called *A ƭat Roog*, meaning “the way of the Divine,” “path of God” or “religious life.” Its supreme deity is Roog, also called Rog, while Cangin-language speakers use Koox. Religious practice includes veneration and offerings to the pangool, ancestral spirits and saints; initiation rites; folk medicine; divination; ancient chants and poems; and preservation of Serer history and identity.

About 85% of Serers are Muslim in contemporary times, while others are Christian and some continue to follow Serer spiritual beliefs. The sources describe a long history of resistance to Islamization and later conversion, including participation in Sufi Muslim brotherhoods such as the Mouride and Tijaniyyah Tariqas.
